cards.front: What is the difference between a compiler and an interpreter?
cards.back: A compiler translates the whole source program into object or machine code before it runs, producing an executable. An interpreter translates and executes the program one statement at a time and produces no standalone executable.

keyPoints.text: compiler translates the whole program first
interpreter translates and executes line by line
a compiler produces an executable

mcq.correct: A compiler translates the whole source program into object or machine code before it runs, producing an executable. An interpreter translates and executes the program one statement at a time and produces no standalone executable.
distractors: A compiler runs the program directly while an interpreter produces object code
An interpreter translates the whole program first, a compiler works line by line
A compiler only works on high-level languages and an interpreter only on assembly

cards.explanation: The difference is when translation happens: all at once, before execution, or repeatedly, during it.

cards.back: A translator that converts assembly language into machine code. Assembly is a low-level language with essentially a one-to-one correspondence between its mnemonics and the processor's instructions.

keyPoints.text: translates assembly language into machine code
one-to-one correspondence with machine instructions

cards.explanation: A compiler works on a high-level language where one statement typically becomes many instructions, so an assembler is not just a compiler for assembly.

cards.front: State one advantage and one disadvantage of compiling rather than interpreting a program.
cards.back: Advantage: the object code is translated once, so it runs faster and can be distributed without the source. Disadvantage: every change needs a full recompile, so the edit-test cycle is slower and platform-specific builds are needed.

keyPoints.text: faster execution
source code is not needed at run time
slower development cycle
the executable is platform specific

cards.explanation: The trade-off is run-time speed against development speed, which is why large systems are compiled and scripts are interpreted.

cards.front: Name the main stages a compiler passes a source program through.
cards.back: Lexical analysis, syntax analysis, semantic analysis, intermediate code generation, optimisation and target code generation.

keyPoints.text: lexical analysis
syntax analysis
semantic analysis
intermediate code generation
optimisation
target code generation

cards.explanation: Lexical analysis turns characters into tokens, syntax analysis checks they form valid structures, and semantic analysis checks they mean something, such as types matching.

cards.front: What do the linker and the loader each do?
cards.back: The linker combines separately compiled object files and libraries into one executable, resolving references between them. The loader copies that executable into memory so the processor can run it.

keyPoints.text: linker combines object files and libraries
produces a single executable
loader places the executable in memory

cards.explanation: Linking is why a program can call a library routine it never contained the source for.

cards.front: What is bytecode, and what role does a virtual machine play?
cards.back: Bytecode is an intermediate instruction set produced by a compiler that is not specific to any processor. A virtual machine interprets or just-in-time compiles it on the machine it is running on.

keyPoints.text: bytecode is intermediate, platform independent code
a virtual machine executes it on the local hardware
write once, run anywhere
synonyms: the same bytecode runs on any machine with a VM

mcq.correct: Platform-independent intermediate code executed by a virtual machine
distractors: Machine code produced by an assembler
Source code that has been minified
Encrypted machine code that only one processor can run

cards.explanation: This is how Java achieves portability: `javac` produces bytecode once, and any machine with a suitable JVM runs it. The cost is that the VM is an extra layer, and the benefit beyond portability is that a just-in-time compiler can optimise for the actual processor at run time using information the original compiler did not have.

cards.front: What is a symbol table, and when is it built?
cards.back: A table the translator keeps of every identifier in the program with its type, scope and, where relevant, its memory address. It is built during the semantic analysis stage and updated as declarations are read.

keyPoints.text: a table of identifiers
with their type and scope
built during semantic analysis

mcq.correct: A table of identifiers with type and scope, built during semantic analysis
distractors: A table of machine instructions, built during code generation
A list of syntax errors, built during lexical analysis
A table of memory addresses for the operating system, built at load time

cards.explanation: The symbol table is what lets the translator answer 'has this name been declared?' and 'is it being used with the right type?', which is why it must be built before those questions are asked. Scope matters because the same name in two functions refers to two different entries. It is also what the linker later uses to match calls to definitions.

cards.front: At which stage of translation is each of these caught: a misspelled keyword, a use of an undeclared variable, and an unmatched bracket?
cards.back: A misspelled keyword and an unmatched bracket are caught in lexical and syntax analysis respectively; a use of an undeclared variable is caught in semantic analysis.

keyPoints.text: a misspelled keyword is a lexical or syntax error
synonyms: not a valid token or statement

keyPoints.text: an unmatched bracket is a syntax error
an undeclared variable is a semantic error
synonyms: the code is grammatically valid but meaningless

distractors: All three are caught by the linker
Semantic, syntax, then lexical analysis
All three are caught at run time

cards.explanation: An unmatched bracket breaks the grammar, so the parser rejects it. An undeclared variable is grammatically perfect - `total = total + 1` is a valid statement whatever `total` is - so only a check against the symbol table catches it. Errors that survive translation and only appear when the program runs are the most expensive, which is what static typing is designed to prevent.

cards.front: Distinguish source code, object code and machine code.
cards.back: Source code is what the programmer writes in a high-level language. Object code is the translated output of the compiler, containing machine instructions with unresolved references to other modules. Machine code is the fully linked, loadable executable the processor runs.

keyPoints.text: source code is written by the programmer
object code has unresolved references
machine code is the linked executable the processor runs

mcq.correct: Source: written. Object: translated but unlinked. Machine: linked and runnable
distractors: Source: written. Object: encrypted. Machine: interpreted
All three mean the same thing at different stages of the same file
Source: written. Object: linked. Machine: compressed

cards.explanation: The gap between object code and machine code is exactly what the linker fills: each module is compiled separately into object code, and the linker resolves the calls between them and adds the library routines. This is why changing one file in a large project means recompiling that file and relinking, rather than recompiling everything.

cards.front: What is just-in-time compilation, and what advantage does it have over pure interpretation?
cards.back: Code is compiled to machine code at run time, typically the first time a method is called or once it is found to run often. It runs much faster than interpretation because the processor executes native instructions rather than the interpreter working through them.

keyPoints.text: compilation happens at run time
hot code is compiled and cached
it runs faster than interpretation

mcq.correct: Compiled at run time; executes native code so it is much faster
distractors: Compiled before execution; runs slower than an interpreter
Interpreted line by line but with caching
Compiled at run time and therefore slower

cards.explanation: A JIT can also optimise using information only available at run time - which branch is usually taken, which types actually occur - something an ahead-of-time compiler cannot know. The cost is a delay the first time a piece of code runs while it compiles, and higher memory use for the compiled code. The JVM and .NET both work this way.

cards.front: Why does an assembler need two passes over the source?
cards.back: The first pass builds a table of labels and the addresses they correspond to; the second pass generates the code, using that table to fill in the addresses the first pass could not yet know.

keyPoints.text: the first pass collects the labels and their addresses
the second pass generates the machine code
synonyms: uses the table from pass one

keyPoints.text: a jump target may appear before its label is defined
synonyms: the address is not yet known

mcq.correct: Pass one collects labels, pass two generates code with the addresses filled in
distractors: Pass one checks syntax, pass two checks semantics
Pass one compiles, pass two optimises
Pass one runs on the CPU, pass two on the GPU

cards.explanation: Consider `JMP end` written near the top of a program where the label `end` is defined at the bottom: the address simply is not known until the whole file has been read. A single-pass assembler would have to leave a gap and patch it later, which is what a linker does at a larger scale. The same two-pass structure appears in any translator that has to resolve forward references.

cards.front: Give two reasons why an interpreted language is easier to debug than a compiled one.
cards.back: Errors are reported against the original source line rather than against generated machine code, and code can be changed and re-run immediately without a separate compile step.

keyPoints.text: errors point at the original source line
synonyms: no mapping back from machine code

keyPoints.text: no compile step, so changes can be tested immediately

mcq.correct: Errors map to the source, and changes need no recompile
distractors: Interpreters run faster, and use less memory
Interpreted code cannot contain logic errors
The interpreter fixes errors automatically

cards.explanation: A compiled program's crash refers to a machine address that has to be mapped back through debug symbols to find the source line, and every change needs a rebuild before it can be tested. Both costs disappear under an interpreter. The counterweight is that a compiler reports every error it finds in one pass, whereas an interpreter only reaches an error when execution gets there.
